The confidence intervals widen as the forecast horizon increases because uncertainty grows the further out we look into the future. In the short term, random fluctuations and smaller-scale variability are more contained and predictable, resulting in narrower intervals. However, over longer time frames, more variables and potential influences come into play—these could include market trends, external shocks, or changes in underlying dynamics—all of which make the outcomes harder to pin down. Specific risks or events could push outcomes outside the stated intervals, particularly if they are sudden, rare, or extreme. Likewise, unexpected positive events, such as breakthroughs in innovation, favorable economic data, or major organizational successes, could drive outcomes well above the upper bounds of the intervals. These risks are inherently difficult to predict and might not be fully captured in a probabilistic framework based on past trends or assumptions of normal variability.
